analysis.one_liner: Requires farm employers to protect workers from wildfire smoke and extreme heat with respirators, water, cooling, and rest breaks.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee since August 2025 with no cosponsors and no committee action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create enforceable federal workplace safety rules for farmworkers exposed to wildfire smoke and extreme heat. Employers would have to provide certified respirators when air quality turns dangerous, water and cooling facilities during dangerous heat, training in languages workers understand, and paid rest breaks of at least 10 minutes every two hours in shaded areas when conditions are bad. The Labor Department would write a permanent standard at least as strict as the toughest state rule, and the protections would take effect immediately even before that rule is finished.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 2 million farmworkers who harvest the country's food would gain immediate, enforceable protection from two hazards that can kill: wildfire smoke containing toxic particulates, and heat waves like the June 2021 Oregon event that killed more than 100 people, including a farmworker [S2]. They would get certified respirators, water and cooling stations, training in their own language, rest breaks in the shade, and legal protection against being punished for asserting these rights [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Farmworkers outdoors in smoke and heat

how_it_helps.text: Employers must give farmworkers N95 or N100 respirators when wildfire smoke makes air dangerous, and mandatory use when it becomes extremely dangerous [S2].
Employers must provide water and cooling facilities during dangerous heat, with mandatory use at extremely dangerous levels [S2].
When air quality or heat reaches dangerous levels, farmworkers get at least 10 minutes of rest every two hours in shaded areas with less smoke or heat [S2].
Workers get training in a language they understand, including indigenous languages, on using the equipment and recognizing heat and smoke illness [S2].
The rules are enforced like any other workplace safety standard, including protection against being fired or punished for complaining [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Agricultural employers would pay for respirators, cooling equipment, training in multiple languages, and mandatory rest breaks during dangerous conditions, though they could get free technical assistance and sample training materials from the Labor Department to help comply [S2].

drawbacks.text: Employers bear the cost of buying respirators, providing water and cooling facilities, and pausing work for mandatory 10-minute rest breaks every two hours when conditions turn dangerous — a real expense for farms operating on thin margins [S2].

The Secretary of Labor would set the air-quality and heat thresholds that trigger mandatory equipment use and rest breaks, giving a federal agency significant discretion over when farmwork must slow or stop [S2].
The interim protections take effect only if the bill becomes law, and as a single-sponsored bill sitting in committee, it may never take effect at all [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and large for a small, vulnerable workforce: N95 respirators, water, shade, rest breaks, and training during dangerous smoke and heat, backed by the same enforcement machinery as any other workplace safety rule [S2]. The strongest objection is cost and rigidity for farm employers — mandatory respirator use and rest breaks on dangerous days, with the Labor Secretary setting the thresholds — though the bill lets employers seek technical assistance and build on existing state standards [S2]. A second, fair objection is durability: with no cosponsors and the bill stalled in committee, the protections exist only on paper.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee and nothing has happened since — no cosponsors, no hearing, no vote.

narrative.text: Introduced August 1, 2025, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Workforce [S4].
No member of either party has signed on as a cosponsor [S3].
As of the latest action record, the committee has taken no further steps — no markup, no hearing, no vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained: farmworkers remain without federal heat and smoke protections, and employers face no new costs. The outcome preserves the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farm employers, who face no new rules

for.name: Rep. Maxine Dexter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and is its only sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no cosponsors from either party and no floor vote has occurred, so no partisan split has been tested; it sits with a Republican-majority committee that has not acted on it [S3, S1].

industries.note: Farms would have to buy protective equipment, provide water and cooling, and give mandatory rest breaks when smoke or heat turns dangerous, plus training materials [S2]. The bill offers federal technical assistance and model training materials to ease compliance [S2].
A new federal mandate for N95/N100 respirators and cooling equipment for farmworkers would create demand for certified protective gear [S2].

analysis.trajectory: The bill has no cosponsors and has sat in committee since August 2025 with no hearings or markup. Single-sponsor workplace safety bills referred to the Education and Workforce Committee rarely advance, so its most likely path is dying quietly at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote.
